final_answer:
LIMITATION: primary-source sites (Cornell, govinfo, house.gov, ussc.gov) were blocked by the egress proxy, so no authority was fetched and verified; the answer below rests on my unverified recall of the statutes and Guidelines and is labeled accordingly.

Short answer: the office that can charge the doctor with (and prove) the larger share of the fraud, meaning the district where the greater intended or actual loss, the greater number of executions, and any serious-bodily-injury facts (20-year max instead of 10 under 1347) occurred. If the two states are roughly equal, the choice barely matters to the Guidelines result.

Reasoning (unverified recall): (1) Venue: each execution of a 1347 scheme is a separate offense, and an office can ordinarily only charge executions that occurred in its own district (18 U.S.C. 3237(a) could allow one district to reach conduct if claims moved through it by interstate commerce, but that is not assured). (2) Under USSG 1B1.3(a)(2), losses from the same course of conduct or common scheme are relevant conduct even if uncharged, and under 3D1.2(d)/2B1.1 fraud counts group and loss is aggregated. So whichever office indicts, its Guidelines range should reflect the loss from both states, assuming the conduct qualifies as the same course of conduct. (3) The statutory maximum is 10 years per count, and 5G1.2(d) stacking applies only to the extent the range exceeds the highest single-count maximum; so the district with more counts has more stacking capacity and is the better vehicle. (4) If a second district later prosecutes, USSG 5G1.3(b) requires a concurrent term and credit when the first term's conduct was fully taken into account as relevant conduct, so a second prosecution typically adds little prison time. Thus the best single vehicle for maximum time is one indictment, in the district with more counts/loss/injury facts, covering all reachable conduct. The facts do not say which district that is, so I cannot name South Carolina or Southern District of Georgia.
